newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - firm in fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - firm in fourth quarter.

text.p: Fourth quarter demand should encourage a strong market for Gulf product prices and premiums as buyers secure heating needs, Gulf traders said on Thursday.

Middle distillate markets are well placed to stay in sight of post-Gulf War price highs as Asian and Mediterranean demand for incremental cargoes from the Gulf picks up during the start of the northern hemisphere's winter, market sources said.
"Demand is already clearly showing its face...together with the tight supplies we're seeing concerns around the market on inventory levels," one Gulf trader said.
"Any supply disruption would turn out be critical," another trader said, referring to Gulf refineries and export ports.

The bullish effect of unexpected cold weather snaps or prolonged cool temperatures was reflected in Gulf premiums last winter when kerosene premiums to independent quotes rallied from 35 cents last September to $1.45 by the end of the year.
Kerosene prices in the same period surged 35 percent.
Gulf kerosene premiums were assessed around 80 cents on Thursday, fanned by good Asian demand which pulled cargoes to $28.15 a barrel fob Gulf, traders said.
Naphtha was assessed at $190.75 a tonne fob Gulf, led to its highest level since August 1992 on the back of strong Far East petrochemical demand.
Gas oil demand from the Mediterranean and northwest Europe is also expected to underpin the Gulf market with cargoes offered more than $1 a barrel over quotes.
Interest is also coming from the India Oil Corp which has tendered for 90,000 tonnes of 0.25 percent sulphur diesel with bids closing October 4.
Key product exporter Saudi Aramco has begun negotiations with term lifters for 1997 supplies against the backdrop of firm prices.
Interested companies have until the end of the month to submit their initial volume and price ideas for the range of Aramco's export slate by early next month.

The seesaw fortunes of Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations may also come to dominate the fourth quarter if Iraqi crude and products hit the market for the first time since its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Wednesday that he had written to U.N. Secretary Boutros Boutros-Ghali that the oil deal be implemented immediately.

Boutros-Ghali called off the implementaion of the deal after Kurdish fighting in northern Iraq and U.S. missile strikes in southern Iraq, saying the safety of inspectors and monitors in charge of the deal could not be guaranteed.
